The second method is the development of the signless concentration.

It seems therefore that by developing the signless concentration, these thoughts and concepts do not get an opportunity due to the very fact that signs fade away.
It is because of our samsaric habit of taking in signs that thoughts and proliferations rise in us.
But even in our endeavor to liberate our minds from thoughts and proliferations, we cannot help resorting to a particular mode of taking in signs.
We have often mentioned the reason why the Buddha proclaimed the middle path.
It is in the nature of some things that though they have to be given up, they cannot be fully dispensed with.
The middle path itself becomes a gradual path because there has to be a graded system in the cause of practice to be followed.

If we have to present the fundamental idea behind these two terms, the middle path and the gradual path, we may say that the cause of practice leading to Nibbana is in principle both pragmatic and relative.
It is pragmatic in the sense that it has a practical value as it is directed towards some gods.
However, it is relative to the extent that the stages that go to make up the path have no absolute value in themselves.
Each stage has only a relative value, being of significance in relation to the next stage.
Every stage in the graded path is dependent and relative.

So even in the attempt to debride the mind from its hold on science,
we cannot help making use of a particular set of science.
In that attempt, we have to be guided by the first principles of relativity and pragmatism.
In order to explain these first principles, we made use of a certain simile in one of our earlier sermons.
The simile is sharpening a razor.
To refresh our memory, the main purpose of bringing up this simile
was to show the difference between meditative reflection,
sammasana, and dogmatic adherence, paramasana.
Whereas paramasana means tenacious grasping,
sammasana is a particular way of holding lightly for some subtle purpose.
It took up the razor simile to illustrate the distinction between the two.
If one grabs the razor roughly and moves it up and down the wedgestone,
it would get blunt.
But if one catches hold of the razor in a relaxed, nonchalant way
and mindfully sweeps the wedgestone back and forth,
it would get sharpened.
This way of reflection on preparations for sankharas reminds us of the two terms
vipassana, insight, and anupassana, contemplation,
which again are relevant to the theme of pragmatism and relativity.
As an illustration, let us take the case of a carpenter planing a piece of wood.
In the process of planing, from time to time,
he might hold up the piece of wood to his left eye
and with his right eye closed, might give it a critical glance.
There is something sinister about this way of looking.
It is as if an expert is detecting a fault-finding critical glance
on the work of an inexpert.
But here it is the carpenter himself, looking at his own artefact.
Why does he do so?
He is himself playing the role of a critic
in order to find out his shortcomings as a carpenter.
If he complacently looks at it with excessive self-confidence,
he can never rectify his errors and improve himself.
In the two terms vipassana and anupassana,
we have a special way of seeing that is penetrative
as well as contemplative.
It is, in short, an objective approach to understand the subjective in one's experience.
It is, in short, an objective approach to understand the subjective in one's experience
with a view to attaining perfection.

That is what a carpenter is doing.
This meditative carpenter too has to direct a critical glance at the preparations in order to find out their shortcomings.
He has to look upon them as alien Parato.
That is the significance of the expression Kaya Nupassi.
If he starts off with the prejudice, this is my body, what is wrong with it?
There is little chance that he will see its shortcomings, its impermanent suffering, not-self characteristics.
If he is to see them, he has to adjust his point of view.
He has to look upon the body as alien Parato.
From this alien point of view, the meditative carpenter not only discovers the shortcomings in his artifact,
but also adopts a technique of planing to smoothen out the rough edges.
What are these rough edges?
The protuberances of craving, conceits and fears.

One can split it up as arupa plus sanyi, whereas a plus rupa sanyi, a signifying negation
equivalent to na.
In the first case, it gives the meaning, percipient of the immaterial self.
In the second case, the meaning is, devoid of perception of form.
There is a subtle difference between these two possible senses.
The commentarial interpretation prefers the first sense, trying to establish the term
arupa as an epithet for Nibbana rather arbitrarily.
It is the second possible interpretation that fits the context.

exercising thoughts, it seems thoughts avitaka are comparable to the army of mara. In this concern,
the important issue of thoughts, so relevant to the life of a meditator, finds an interesting answer.
The army of mara is, in the last analysis, our thoughts themselves. Generally, we take references
to an army of mara in its gross sense. But in some sutras, like the padhana sutra in the sutra nipata,
the army of mara is defined in terms of thoughts. For instance, one reads in the padhana sutra,
kama te padhana sena, dhutiya arati vujyati, tatiya kupipasa te, catu te tannha pavujyati. Sense desires are your
first battalion, and boredom is reckoned the second. Hunger and thirst comes as the third, and craving is called
the fourth. The word kama in this context does not refer to pleasurable objects as such, though that is
what is usually meant by it. Rather, it refers to thoughts about pleasurable objects. In fact,
kama in its real sense does imply thoughts about pleasurable objects, as clearly stated in the
following words of the Sanyutani Kaya. They are not the pleasures, those charming things in the world.
Trustful thought is the pleasure of all men. They go on as before,
all those charming things in the world. But it is the desire for them that the wise discipline.
As we already mentioned in our discussion of the Satka Panya Sutra, desire is the cause of thinking.
There, the relation between desire and thought is recognized. It is the desire for pleasure that those
who are prudently wise discipline and despair. All this goes to prove that the word
prama primarily refers not to the objects of sense desire, but to thoughts about them. So,
in the last analysis, we are confronted with the question of thought.
For instance, hunger and thirst, Kupipasa are cited as another battalion of Mar.
Here too, it is not hunger and thirst in themselves that represent the army of Mar.
It is thoughts about them, such as Kinsu Asissam, Ikuangwa Asissam,
What shall I eat? Where shall I eat? For we read in the Sari Bhutta Sutta of the Sutta Nipata,
What shall I eat? Where shall I eat? Badly have I slept? Where shall I sleep? Such miserable thoughts did the trainee discipline,
as he wanders forth without any boy. Against this background of the paramount importance attached to thoughts,
we can reassess the significance of the following verse in the Bodhi Vag of the Udana we had already quoted in a previous sermon.
When phenomena manifest themselves to the resolutely meditating Brahmin,
he stands fumigating the hordes of Mar, even as the sun irradiating the firmament.
After his enlightenment, the Buddha spent the first week seated under the Bodhi tree,
and during the last week of the night of the seventh day, reflected on the law of dependent arising,
both in the direct and reverse order. This joyous utterance has an allusion to it.
It is when the insight into conditioned phenomena dawns on the contemplating arahant,
that he smokes out the hordes of Mar, like the sun illuminating the sky.
In the light of this simile, we can now understand how the hordes of Mar are dispelled.
It is the reflection on the law of dependent arising in direct and reverse order
that dispels the denizens of darkness of ignorance, namely thoughts.
The principle underlying the law of dependent arising is summed up in the following abstract formula which we had discussed at length.
This being, this comes to be. With the arising of this, this arises. This not being, this does not come to be.
With the cessation of this, this ceases. When this principle is applied in a thorough-going way to conditioned phenomena,
they tend to fade away. That is how thoughts are dispelled. In the 12-linked formula, each pair of,
for example, avidya-pachya-sankhara, is based on this dynamic principle represented by the term pachya.
A penetrative reflection into arising and ceasing, in a flash, deprives thoughts of their evocative power
and renders them dugatory. This is the smoking out of the army of Mara, the thoughts.
Now to hark back to the avitaka-samadhi, we come across an allusion to it in the Sariputta Theragata.
The fully awakened one's disciple, on attaining to thoughtless musing, is at once endowed with silence that is of the ennobling type.
Now, this avitaka-samadhi, then, is none other than the arhatthapala-samadhi, which is known as
aryotunni bhavo, noble silence. This is not to be confused with the second jhana, in which thinking and pondering
have been calmed down by samatha, tranquility meditation. Noble silence, in the highest sense,

We get another allusion to this thoughtless concentration in Vimalatheri gatha.
Nisina-arukha-mulamhi, avitaka-samadhi. Seated am I at the root of a tree, a winner to the thoughtless state.
We come across a long verse in the dhita-rosutta of the mara-samuyutta, in the samyutta-nikaya, where again there is a reference to this thoughtless concentration.
In body relaxed, in mind well-freed, concocting not, mindful, eboodless, while knowing the norm, he muses thoughtless.
All this points to the fact that the arhatthapala-samadhi is called avitaka-samadhi in a very special sense.
It is relevant to inside meditation, and not to mere tranquility meditation.
The problem of thoughts could be fully resolved only when the reckonings born of prolific perception are abandoned.
In the Chulamagga of the Udana, we get a reference to the Arhatthapala-samadhi.

Tenakopanasamayena Bhagavā attenu papancha sannyā saṅkha pahaṇa pachavikhamānu nishinu moti.
At that time the fortunate one was seated reflecting on his abandonment of recollings born of prolific perceptions.
At that time the mind is free from worldly concepts born of prolific perception,
and inwardly all thoughts are rendered powerless.
Thoughts do not come up and there is no grasping of science.
It is to highlight this fact that the terms avitaka jhana and avitaka samadhi are used.
By way of further proof, he may cite the following two verses in the Sanyojana Sutra
of the Sagātaka Vagya in the Sanyojana Nikāl.
Our deity poses the question,
What is the fetter of the world?
What is it straying along?
By giving up what do they say?
Nibbāna is attained.
And the Buddha gives the answer.
To delight and fretted is the world.
Thought is its trailing along.
It is that craving.
By giving up which they say Nibbāna is attained.
Here again we have an indication of the relevance of thoughts to the question of insight.
The Sundarika Bhāradvāja Sutra of the Suthanipāta has the following allusion to the qualities of an arhant.
Bhavāsava yasa vachikkhara che vidhupita atthagata nasanti.
In whom the influxes of existence and the sediments of speech as well are smoked out, gone down and exist no more.
The commentary takes the word vachikhara to mean harsh speech.
There is some imbalance between the two terms, bhavasava and vachikhara, if the commentarial interpretation is granted.
Harsh speech could ill afford to get coupled with influxes of existence to be cited as fundamental defilements extinct in an arhan.
It seems vachikhara has a deeper significance than that.
It probably means the sediments or dregs, Sanskrit char, or speech, namely the worldly concepts and designations,
which, as Papandhaswanya-sankha, a reckoning born of prolific perception, form the basis of all thoughts.
In the arhan, therefore, influxes of existence, as well as sediments of speech, are smocked out, grown down, and made extinct.
This, then, seems to be the most plausible interpretation of the two lines in question.
So, we have garnered sufficient canonical evidence to conclude that the terms sitakka and papancha are particularly relevant to the life of a meditator.
Also, the fact that the arhatapala samadhi has been called avitakka samadhi shows that the conquest of thoughts is not of a temporary type as in the case of tranquility meditation.
On the other hand, it is a transcendence of a more radical type.
Through an insight into the relative variety of worldly concepts, they are falsifying nature and the perception of permanence underlying them.
Avitakka samadhi is a term used to denote that state of complete emancipation of the mind by making all signs fade away,
so that the whole world appears like a blood-watercolour painting,
thus freeing the mind from the perception of diversity without even resorting to perception of unity.
